newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: New Argentine alliance launches Menem challenge.
newsitem.headline: New Argentine alliance launches Menem challenge.

text.p: Argentina's new opposition alliance made its public debut on Wednesday with an 18-point "emergency program" aimed at the twin perils dogging President Carlos Menem's government -- unemployment and corruption.

The centre-left alliance of the century-old Radical Party and young Frepaso coalition burst upon the political scene this weekend, drastically altering the outlook for October's mid-term elections in Congress and presidential elections in 1999.
The ruling Peronist Party's majority in the lower house of Congress is at risk for the first time, as is the Peronist succession when Menem steps down after two terms in 1999.
"This is not about winning an election but about building power so that in 1999 we can really govern this country," the Radical ex-President Raul Alfonsin told a news conference.

"We have given joy to many millions of compatriots. The Argentine people can once again feel that a different country is possible," said Frepaso deputy Carlos Alvarez, who tops the alliance's list of deputies for Buenos Aires in October.

An opinion poll by Mori shows the alliance has indeed been welcomed: 77 percent of people in Buenos Aires Province, home to 40 percent of Argentina's voters, said it was a "positive or very positive" development.
But a 55 percent majority also cautioned the alliance not to meddle with Menem's 1991 decision to peg the peso to the U.S. dollar, a move which is credited with bringing zero inflation and stability.
The last years of Alfonsin's rule saw economic chaos, with inflation near 5,000 percent in 1989, when Menem took over.
Inflation is now zero and investment has poured in, but unemployment has rocketed to 16.1 percent sparking roadblocks and protests, with another general strike due on Aug. 14.

Menem, his popularity waning, has compared the alliance to the "sinister" coalition against party founder Juan Peron in 1946. He has raised the spectre of a return to the days of hourly price rises, endless lines and food riots.

"It is a purely electioneering alliance plotted behind the backs of the Argentine people," he said in Bolivia on Wednesday. "It repeats other alliances which in eight years of government have not hurt Peronism in the slightest."
But, with political analysts agreeing Menem's electoral nightmare has come true, the new alliance was in a party mood.
"The centre of power has trembled. The opposition has alligned, it has united to triumph," said Buenos Aires city's Radical mayor Fernando de La Rua.

The invective was aimed at what Alvarez called "a climate of moral decadence such as has never been seen in Argentina's living memory," and at the "concentration of wealth" reaped from Menem's privatisations and free-market reforms.

The 18-point parliamentary programme, which the alliance called an "emergency programme for the present day," promised to ensure independent courts, new laws and a commission to combat corruption, as well as work on job creation and tax breaks on basic foodstuffs.

But it was careful to respect currency stability. Even Alfonsin, once a critic of pegging the peso to the dollar, said scrapping it would be a "catastrophe -- because not only are 50 percent of people's savings in dollars, but the business world's too."
